summary: Give the TV mounting height calculator the watching height, the viewing angle and the tilt angle (Φ) and it returns horizontal watching distance (HWD). That makes it useful for whatever you happen to be working on. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the TV mounting height calculator work?
sections.html:
The TV mounting height calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports horizontal watching distance (HWD) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the watching distance options); then you type in the watching height (WH), the viewing angle (Watching parameters), the tilt angle (Φ) (Watching parameters) and the tilt angle (Φ) (Watching parameters).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the TV mounting height calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Horizontal watching distance (HWD)=(TV height (TVH) − watching height (WH)) ÷ the tangent of (tilt angle (Φ))
Watching distance optimal (VD)=(TV height (TVH) − watching height (WH)) ÷ the tangent of (tilt angle (Φ))
Viewing angle=2 × ((8 ÷ 337) × the square root of (337) × screen size ÷ watching distance optimal (VD))
TV height (TVH)=TV bottom edge height + (9 ÷ 674) × the square root of (337) × screen size
Optimal watching distance (HWD)=(watching distance optimal (VD))
Horizontal watching distance (HWD)=(8 ÷ 337) × the square root of (337) × screen size ÷ the tangent of ((1 ÷ 2) × viewing angle)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The TV mounting height calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the watching height, the viewing angle and the tilt angle (Φ) — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the TV mounting height calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns horizontal watching distance (HWD), derived from the watching height, the viewing angle and the tilt angle (Φ). Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the TV mounting height calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the watching height, the viewing angle and the tilt angle (Φ), which is 7 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter screen size in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Screen size opens in inches and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the TV mounting height calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
